instruction.text: Select the two objects the Romans used for cleaning.

feedback.finish: The Romans cared a lot about personal hygiene! They also used tweezers and razors to tidy their hair, and toothpicks and powders to keep their teeth clean.

atoms.b: The Romans used a ((++curved straight)) metal scraper called a strigil to remove sweat, dirt and oil from the skin after exercise or bathing. This helped keep their bodies ((++clean dirty)) before the widespread use of soap.
atoms.sound: The Romans used a curved metal scraper, called a streejil, to remove sweat, dirt and oil from the skin after exercise or bathing. This helped keep their bodies clean before the widespread use of soap.

atoms.b: In public bathrooms, you could also find a xylospongium. This was a sea ((++sponge weed)) attached to a wooden stick, stored in a bucket of vinegar or salt water.
atoms.sound: In public bathrooms, you could also find a xylospunjium. This was a sea sponge attached to a wooden stick, stored in a bucket of vinegar or salt water.

atoms.b: Historians are not entirely sure what it was used for, but it was likely either for cleaning ((++toilets bedrooms)) or Roman bottoms!

feedback.finish: Open-plan public toilets were a common feature of Roman cities. Much like bathhouses, they were a space where Romans would hold meetings, catch up with friends and share news and gossip.

atoms.text: In 1972, builders in York uncovered the remains of an underground sewer system, which had been used by the Romans to move dirty water and waste away from buildings. This helped keep the streets of Roman cities cleaner and reduced the risk of diseases.

The sewers included pipes as well as larger tunnels made from materials like clay and stone. In some places, the passages were wide enough for enslaved people to be sent inside to maintain the system by moving waste and clearing debris.

atoms.a: What was the main purpose of the sewer system?
What materials were used to build the sewer tunnels?
